To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) SAMe is an essential metabolite for the liver that is required for the synthesis of phospholipids, the detoxification of xenobiotics, the maintenance of redox homeostasis, and the regulation of the cell cycle; (2) SAM is the methyl donor for transmethylation reactions; (3) the liver is the major site for SAM synthesis; (4) the major SAM synthesis enzyme in the liver, MAT, is transcriptionally regulated by the nuclear receptor,

(1) the development of NASH is due to the impaired synthesis of SAMe, which is the major methyl donor in the liver, and (2), as a consequence of this defect, transmethylation reactions that generate PC and creatine are impaired, which leads to the accumulation of toxic methyl acceptors (diacylglycerol and guanidinoacetate) and to the development of NACH.

the liver receptor homolog (LRH-1) is a key transcriptional activator of the genes that encode enzymes involved in methionine metabolism and that LRH-1 is required to prevent the spontaneous development of NALFD in Mat1a-deficient mice, a model that recapitulates the human condition of SAMe deficiency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of the molecular mechanisms involved in the regulation of transmethylation flux and its role in the pathophysiology of NASH and HCC.
the identification of new molecular mechanisms that underlie the pathogenesis of NASH, the most common cause of cirrhosis and HCC.
the role of liver receptor homolog (LRH)-1, a member of the nuclear receptor family of transcription factors, in the regulation of hepatic transmethylation flux and the development of NASH.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
(1) transmethylation flux is essential for the maintenance of liver homeostasis and (2) its impairment, by any means, leads to the development of NASH.

(1) SAMe is the active methyl donor for transmethylation reactions, (2) GNMT is the major enzyme involved in SAMe catabolism, (3) GNMT deficiency results in increased SAMe availability, (4) increased SAMe availability leads to decreased transmethylation flux, (5) decreased transmethylation reactions result in increased methylation fluxes to SAMe and (6) increased methylation flux to SAMe leads to increased SAMe availability.
“the liver is the organ responsible for the synthesis and metabolism of methyl groups and that SAMe and GNMT deficiency is the main factor leading to NASH and HCC.”
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the liver plays a central role in methyl metabolism, that methyl balance is critical for liver function, and that methyl metabolism is a key regulator of liver disease.

we have shown that the liver is a central organ for the control of methionine and transmethylation homeostasis and that SAMe deficiency is sufficient to induce NALSH, HCC, and liver fibrosis, which are the hallmarks of the metabolic syndrome, and that the liver is an important organ for the control, through the transcription factor, LRH-1 (liver receptor homolog 2), of transmethylation flux.

we have demonstrated that SAMe is a critical methyl donor for hepatic methionine and cholinemetabolism and that the liver plays a central role in maintaining methionine and methyl balance in the body.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SAMe and methylation are critical for maintaining liver health.
SAMe and GNMT are essential for maintaining the liver in a noninjured state and that their deficiency can lead to the development of NASH, HCC, and cirrhosis.
the transmethylation pathway is critical in maintaining liver homeostasis and that the liver receptor homolog-1 (LRH-1) transcription factor is a key regulator of the methylation pathway.
